results.name: sparse_rule_member_yes
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all fall in a sparse rule (powers of 2, squares, powers of 3, or cubes), yes rate on non-example targets that belong to a sparse rule containing all the examples; observed < null means people extend the rule to new members less than the model's rule posterior predicts (observed > null: more).
results.code:
# name: sparse_rule_member_yes
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that all fall in a sparse rule (powers of 2, squares, powers of 3, or cubes), yes rate on non-example targets that belong to a sparse rule containing all the examples; observed < null means people extend the rule to new members less than the model's rule posterior predicts (observed > null: more).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    rules = [np.array([1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]), np.arange(1, 11) ** 2, np.array([1, 3, 9, 27, 81]), np.array([1, 8, 27, 64])]
    hit = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for R in rules:
        hit |= np.all(np.isin(E, R) | ~valid, axis=1) & np.isin(t, R)
    m = (n >= 2) & hit & ~in_set
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: sparse_rule_numeric_neighbor_yes
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all fall in one sparse rule (powers of 2, squares, powers of 3, or cubes), yes rate on targets in none of those sparse rules but within 5 of some example; observed > null means people retain numeric-similarity generalisation around rule-like examples that the model (whose rule posterior dominates and rejects non-members) suppresses, observed < null means they reject near neighbours even more.
results.code:
# name: sparse_rule_numeric_neighbor_yes
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that all fall in one sparse rule (powers of 2, squares, powers of 3, or cubes), yes rate on targets in none of those sparse rules but within 5 of some example; observed > null means people retain numeric-similarity generalisation around rule-like examples that the model (whose rule posterior dominates and rejects non-members) suppresses, observed < null means they reject near neighbours even more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    rules = [np.array([1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]), np.arange(1, 11) ** 2, np.array([1, 3, 9, 27, 81]), np.array([1, 8, 27, 64])]
    any_rule = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    t_in_any = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for R in rules:
        all_in = np.all(np.isin(E, R) | ~valid, axis=1)
        any_rule |= all_in
        t_in_any |= np.isin(t, R)
    near = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & any_rule & ~t_in_any & (near >= 1) & (near <= 5)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: last_digit_vs_parity_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples sharing one last digit, among non-example targets of the same parity as the examples, yes rate when the target shares that last digit minus when it does not; observed > null means people use the "ends in d" rule more strongly (relative to odd/even) than the model's family prior predicts, observed < null less.
results.code:
# name: last_digit_vs_parity_contrast
# description: For sets of >=2 examples sharing one last digit, among non-example targets of the same parity as the examples, yes rate when the target shares that last digit minus when it does not; observed > null means people use the "ends in d" rule more strongly (relative to odd/even) than the model's family prior predicts, observed < null less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    d = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin, dmax = np.nanmin(d, axis=1), np.nanmax(d, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (dmin == dmax) & ~in_set & (np.mod(t, 2) == np.mod(dmin, 2))
    same = base & (np.mod(t, 10) == dmin)
    diff = base & (np.mod(t, 10) != dmin)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: interior_proximity_gradient
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples, among non-example targets strictly inside [min,max], yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus targets more than 10 from every example; observed > null means people generalise by similarity to individual examples inside the span (a gradient the model's whole-interval hypotheses, near-flat inside the span, under-produce), observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: interior_proximity_gradient
# description: For sets of >=2 examples, among non-example targets strictly inside [min,max], yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus targets more than 10 from every example; observed > null means people generalise by similarity to individual examples inside the span (a gradient the model's whole-interval hypotheses, near-flat inside the span, under-produce), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    near = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & (near >= 1)
    a, b = base & (near <= 3), base & (near > 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_cell_disagreement
results.description: Over (number_set, target) cells answered by >=2 people, the mean probability that two different responses in the cell disagree (unbiased pairwise disagreement 2k(n-k)/(n(n-1))); observed < null means people are more consistent (p_yes more extreme) than the model's predictions, observed > null means the model's predictions are too confident relative to human disagreement.
results.code:
# name: within_cell_disagreement
# description: Over (number_set, target) cells answered by >=2 people, the mean probability that two different responses in the cell disagree (unbiased pairwise disagreement 2k(n-k)/(n(n-1))); observed < null means people are more consistent (p_yes more extreme) than the model's predictions, observed > null means the model's predictions are too confident relative to human disagreement.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby([df["number_set"].astype(str), df["target"]])["rating"].agg(["sum", "count"])
    g = g[g["count"] >= 2]
    k, n = g["sum"].to_numpy(float), g["count"].to_numpy(float)
    return float(np.mean(2 * k * (n - k) / (n * (n - 1)))) if len(g) else 0.0

results.name: set_size_inrange_contrast
results.description: Among non-example targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples, yes rate for 2-example sets minus yes rate for 4-example sets; observed > null means adding examples tightens/changes generalisation more than the model's size principle predicts (observed < null: less).
results.code:
# name: set_size_inrange_contrast
# description: Among non-example targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples, yes rate for 2-example sets minus yes rate for 4-example sets; observed > null means adding examples tightens/changes generalisation more than the model's size principle predicts (observed < null: less).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~in_set
    a, b = base & (n == 2), base & (n == 4)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: below_minus_above_outside_yes
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-15 outside the examples' [min,max], yes rate for targets below the minimum minus targets above the maximum; observed > null means people extend generalisation toward smaller numbers more than toward larger ones (a log/Weber-like magnitude asymmetry) beyond what the model's linear intervals and stimulus design produce, observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: below_minus_above_outside_yes
# description: Among non-example targets 1-15 outside the examples' [min,max], yes rate for targets below the minimum minus targets above the maximum; observed > null means people extend generalisation toward smaller numbers more than toward larger ones (a log/Weber-like magnitude asymmetry) beyond what the model's linear intervals and stimulus design produce, observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    below = (lo - t >= 1) & (lo - t <= 15)
    above = (t - hi >= 1) & (t - hi <= 15)
    if below.sum() == 0 or above.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[below].mean() - r[above].mean())

results.name: wide_spread_inrange_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples spanning >=60 (max-min), yes rate on targets strictly inside [min,max] that are not examples; observed > null means people still generalise to "almost any number in the span" more than the beta-share width prior (which penalises near-full ranges) predicts, observed < null means they generalise even less.
results.code:
# name: wide_spread_inrange_yes_rate
# description: For sets of >=3 examples spanning >=60 (max-min), yes rate on targets strictly inside [min,max] that are not examples; observed > null means people still generalise to "almost any number in the span" more than the beta-share width prior (which penalises near-full ranges) predicts, observed < null means they generalise even less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (hi - lo >= 60) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~in_set
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0
